_meta.sources: AASM sleep hygiene guidance; VA CBT-I public-domain materials; standard sleep medicine references

caffeine.title: Caffeine Management
key_facts: Caffeine has a half-life of about 5–6 hours — meaning a coffee at 3 PM still has half of its caffeine in your system by 9 PM.
Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, suppressing sleepiness. That's why it's harder to fall asleep when you've had it late.
Even if you think 'caffeine doesn't affect me anymore,' it still degrades your sleep quality, even if you fall asleep.
recommendations: Avoid coffee and strong tea after 2 PM.
Energy drinks often contain even more caffeine than coffee.
If you rely on coffee, try moving your last cup to before noon.
Green tea has less caffeine but still has an effect.
caffeine.alternative: If you need an afternoon lift, try water with lemon, a few minutes of stretching, or a brief walk outside in natural light.

alcohol.title: Alcohol and Sleep
key_facts: Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but it significantly degrades sleep quality — especially REM sleep.
Alcohol suppresses breathing and can worsen sleep apnea.
A few hours after drinking, the sedative effect wears off, often causing fragmented sleep and waking in the early morning.
Alcohol disrupts the natural sleep cycle, making early-morning awakenings more likely.
recommendations: Try to avoid alcohol within 3 hours of bedtime.
If you do drink, aim for 4–5 hours before bed, in moderation.
Don't use alcohol as a sleep aid — it's not real sleep.

exercise.title: Exercise and Sleep
key_facts: Regular exercise improves sleep quality and is one of the most effective sleep hygiene behaviors.
Timing matters — vigorous exercise within 3 hours of bedtime can raise body temperature and activate the nervous system, making it harder to fall asleep.
Physical tiredness after exercise is not the same as sleep readiness.
recommendations: Aim for aerobic exercise in the morning or afternoon.
If evening is the only option, finish at least 2–3 hours before bed.
Suitable pre-sleep movement: gentle yoga, walking, tai chi.
Avoid high-intensity interval training (HIIT) close to bedtime.

screen_light.title: Blue Light and Screens
key_facts: Blue light suppresses melatonin secretion, tricking the brain into thinking it's still daytime.
Short-wavelength blue light from phones, tablets, and computers has the biggest effect on sleep.
Even if the screen doesn't feel bright, it still affects melatonin.
The emotional pull of social media content (anger, anxiety, excitement) also activates the nervous system.
recommendations: Try to put the phone away an hour before bed.
If you can't, enable 'Night Shift' or 'eye-care mode' (warmer color).
Keep the phone out of sight — not on your pillow.
Use a reading lamp instead of your phone screen.

bedroom_environment.title: Bedroom Environment
key_facts: Optimal sleep temperature is around 65–72°F (18–22°C); too hot or too cold disrupts both falling asleep and depth of sleep.
Total darkness supports melatonin — even small lights (electronics, indicators) can interfere.
Noise is a major and underestimated sleep disrupter.
recommendations: Keep the bedroom around 65–72°F.
Use blackout curtains or an eye mask.
Use earplugs or a white-noise machine to mask sound.
Move glowing devices out of the bedroom or cover them.
Choose bedding that feels comfortable to your skin.

sleep_schedule.title: Sleep Schedule
key_facts: Your body has an internal clock (circadian rhythm) that prefers consistency.
Getting up at the same time every day — including weekends — is the single most powerful sleep-regulation behavior.
'Sleep debt' is real, but weekend sleep-ins don't truly repay it.
Even after a bad night, getting up at your usual time matters.
recommendations: Set a fixed wake time, and stick to it even when sleep was rough.
Don't sleep in more than an hour later on weekends.
If you nap, keep it under 30 minutes and no later than 3 PM.
Sleepiness usually arrives in a specific 'sleep window' — going to bed too early or too late disrupts the rhythm.

pre_sleep_routine.title: Pre-Sleep Routine
key_facts: The brain learns by association — a fixed sequence before bed helps it recognize 'time to sleep.'
A wind-down routine doesn't need to be long — 10–30 minutes is plenty.
The key is consistency — the same sequence, in the same order.
recommendations: A simple sequence: dim the lights → prepare tomorrow's basics → worry journal (if needed) → guided breathing → bed.
Keep the bed for sleep only — avoid phones, work, or eating in it.
'Externalize' anxious thoughts — write them down and tell yourself, 'I'll look at this tomorrow.'
